title: Constant-factor approximation of graph crossing number
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\geq1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite undirected graph \(G\), outputs a drawing \(D\) in the plane satisfying \[\operatorname{cr}(D)\leq C\,\operatorname{cr}(G)\] with probability at least \(2/3\)?

context:
Cabello proves that there is a constant \(c_{0}>1\) for which deterministic polynomial-time \(c_{0}\)-approximation is impossible unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), even on cubic graphs. This does not rule out an algorithm with some larger fixed factor. A randomized algorithm is not excluded merely by assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Chuzhoy and Tan give a randomized approximation factor \(2^{O((\log n)^{7/8}\log\log n)}\operatorname{poly}(\Delta)\) for simple graphs with \(n\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\). For bounded degree this is subpolynomial in \(n\), but still does not supply a universal constant.

Solé-Pi’s Theorem 1.2 constructs drawings with \(\operatorname{cr}(G)+O(n^{4}/(\log\log n)^{\delta})\) crossings, for an absolute \(\delta>0\), in randomized polynomial time. This yields asymptotic factor \(1+o(1)\) for dense simple graphs, but the additive error does not yield a constant multiplicative guarantee on arbitrary graphs with small crossing number.

The 2023 paper studies maximizing the number of retained edges subject to a crossing budget. Its conditional hardness for Maximum Bounded-Crossing Subgraph should not be read as hardness of every constant approximation for the minimum total crossings of the entire input graph.
why: Crossing minimization is a basic graph-layout optimization problem with applications to drawing networks and circuit layouts. A constant approximation would establish a general algorithmic guarantee across sparse and dense inputs, beyond the degree-dependent and additive-error bounds currently available.
status_note: Checked the original full question and drawing model, the 2022 full approximation theorem, the distinct 2023 hardness variant, and the 2025/2026 dense-graph theorem. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no universal constant-factor approximation or impossibility covering all constants. The randomized convention is explicit; the historical P ≠ NP hardness is stated only for deterministic algorithms.

progress.text: A fixed-factor inapproximability result establishes an obstruction to arbitrarily accurate polynomial-time approximation.

sentences: Draw every graph in the plane using at most a fixed constant times its minimum possible number of crossings.
The constant must be independent of the graph size and maximum degree.
The algorithm must construct a drawing in polynomial time; bounded-error randomization is allowed.
Existing low-degree and dense-graph results do not provide this guarantee for all graphs.
Hardness for one fixed ratio above one leaves open the possibility of a larger universal constant.

definitions:
The input explicitly lists the vertices and edges of an unweighted graph. Parallel edges are permitted and counted separately, as in the source. Self-loops can be omitted because they can be drawn locally without crossings. There is no bound on degree, genus or crossing number, and no planar subgraph or embedding is provided. Running time is polynomial in the full input length on every random tape.

A drawing places vertices at distinct points and represents each edge by a simple polygonal curve joining its endpoints, without passing through any other vertex. The objective \(\operatorname{cr}(D)\) is the total number of pairwise edge crossings, summed over the entire drawing. The crossing number \(\operatorname{cr}(G)\) is its minimum over all drawings. One may restrict to good drawings: adjacent edges do not cross, two edges cross at most once, and no three edges cross at one point.

The output must specify a drawing, rather than only an unsupported estimate of its value. A finite combinatorial representation suffices: list crossings in order along each original edge and give a planar embedding of the graph obtained by replacing crossings with degree-four vertices. At each such vertex, the two segments of each original edge must be opposite in the cyclic order. This records the original curves and their crossings without requiring real-number coordinates.

Randomization with bounded error is explicitly allowed, in keeping with the later approximation literature; a deterministic algorithm would also qualify. The success probability is over internal coins for each fixed graph. The constant \(C\) and the polynomial time bound are independent of the graph. In particular, a factor depending on its maximum degree does not meet the target. When \(\operatorname{cr}(G)=0\), the approximation guarantee requires a drawing with no crossings.

This is ordinary topological crossing number. Edges need not be straight, there is no prescribed rotation system, and the objective is not the maximum number of crossings on any one edge. The source’s Multiple Edge Insertion problem additionally keeps a specified subgraph planar; that constraint is absent here.
answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm and prove its running time and universal constant-factor guarantee, or prove that none exists. A conditional impossibility result must state its complexity assumption and cover randomized algorithms in the stated model. Hardness for a particular small approximation factor alone does not exclude all constant factors.
